title: Vision: Zero Bugs — Johann Schleier-Smith, Temporal
talk_summary: A vision talk arguing that zero-bug software is achievable by porting aerospace high-assurance practices (independent verification teams, specifications, formal methods, modularity) to agentic coding, since agents make high-assurance code ~100x cheaper. Concrete transferable bits are process patterns: separate prompts/models for code vs. tests, explicit risk analysis/safety cases, and modular small code.

takeaways.technique: Independent verifier via separate prompt/model from the author
takeaways.what_they_do: Mirror aerospace's separate coding and verification teams by using a different prompt (and optionally a different foundation model) to write tests than the one that wrote the code, so the checker doesn't inherit the author's blind spots.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can have separate prompts to the LLM for testing versus for writing the code in the first place

takeaways.technique: Explicit risk analysis / safety case artifact per change
takeaways.what_they_do: Ask the LLM to enumerate what could go wrong and how the code mitigates each, as a qualitative artifact separate from formal proofs.
takeaways.evidence_quote: asking it to write safety cases, which are statements about things that could go wrong and how that thing that could go wrong is being mitigated

takeaways.technique: Modularity and small code as a verification multiplier
takeaways.what_they_do: Argue that modular, small, library-backed code gives linear rather than exponential verification cost, so local reasoning works at every level — for humans, LLMs, and formal tools alike.
takeaways.evidence_quote: As you chain modules together, you get a subexponential scaling, perhaps even a linear scaling rather than an exponential scaling

takeaways.technique: Budget for input/reasoning tokens, not output
takeaways.what_they_do: Break down agentic coding cost and show output tokens are a small fraction; most spend is repeated input and reasoning tokens from test/iterate loops.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the cost to generate the output tokens is only about 15% of the overall cost
takeaways.numbers: ~$2 for a small game; 600k input + 3.5M cached input + 48k reasoning vs 28k output tokens; output ~15% of cost

takeaways.technique: Formal/spec-anchored checks on critical sections only
takeaways.what_they_do: Use inline assertions/proofs (Dafny-style) on small critical functions, verified before the generated code runs, rather than across the whole codebase.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it allows you to put proofs in line with your code, allowing theorem proving software to come along and verify that that code does exactly what you said you wanted to do
takeaways.numbers: verification benchmark success ~30%→~100%, runtime down ~50x over 20 years

takeaways.what_they_do: Emphasize quality-through-process: planning/requirements, independent verification, integration testing, with feedback loops refining each stage — the same discipline needed to keep agents on the rails.
takeaways.evidence_quote: as we're thinking about how agentic coding works, thinking about how we keep agents on the rails and doing what we want them to do, process really is something that we do want to think about
